subject: english-literature
title: Streams and Echoes
welcome_lead: Sometimes the voice flows like a river of thought.
meta_desc: KS3 English Literature adventure on stream of consciousness and voice effects.
final_note: You can now recognise stream of consciousness and voice effects.

concepts.def: Continuous flow of thoughts on page.
Distinct narrator style on the page.

walkthroughs.body_html: Stream of consciousness writes thoughts as they tumble — fragmented, jumping. Virginia Woolf and James Joyce are famous for it.
Tone = how the voice feels (warm, sneering, anxious). Register = formality (formal/informal). Both shape voice.
Dialogue reveals character. The narrator may sound different from the characters — distinct voice at every level.

mcqs.q: Fragmented thoughts tumbling across the page is.
What is the structural framework of The Canterbury Tales?
options: Metaphors are true and similes are false.
It is one continuous story told by Chaucer from beginning to end.
It is a religious text used in Catholic services.
A frame narrative — pilgrims travelling to Canterbury tell stories along the way, allowing Chaucer to juxtapose different voices, genres and social classes.
It means it is wrong to write fiction.
The claim that judging a text by what the author 'intended' is fallacious — the text's meaning lies in the work itself, not the author's stated or guessed intentions.
It means authors can never make mistakes when writing.
Metaphors are true and similes are false.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between a metaphor and a simile?
options: Metaphors are short and similes are long.
It is a religious text used in Catholic services.
Metaphors are true and similes are false.
A simile compares using 'like' or 'as'; a metaphor states one thing IS another, making an implicit comparison without those connectives.
